title: Orthogonal Matrices
description: Day 40: orthogonal matrices, Q^T = Q^{-1}, orthonormal columns and rows, determinant plus or minus 1, preserved lengths and angles, rotations and reflections, tall matrices with orthonormal columns, QR, and a preview of the SVD. 12 questions pulled per attempt.

questions.prompt: A square matrix $Q$ is **orthogonal** if
explanations: That is a *symmetric* matrix. Orthogonal matrices need not be symmetric (e.g. rotations).
That is an involution. It holds for some orthogonal matrices but is not the definition.
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is its transpose, not its negative.

questions.prompt: If $Q$ is orthogonal, then $Q^{-1}=$
explanations: $-Q$ times $Q$ is $-Q^2$, not $I$.
$Q^TQ=I$ is the identity matrix, not an inverse.
That would need $Q^2=I$.

questions.prompt: A square matrix is orthogonal exactly when its columns are
explanations: Independence is far weaker; any invertible matrix has independent columns.
Rows equal to columns means symmetric, which is not required.
The columns must also be *unit* vectors. $\mathrm{diag}(1,2)$ has orthogonal columns but is not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: The $(i,j)$ entry of $Q^TQ$ is
explanations: That is the $(i,j)$ entry of $QQ^T$.
The entries of a product are dot products, not squares of entries.
That is not how matrix products work.

questions.prompt: For a **square** matrix $Q$, which statement is equivalent to $Q$ being orthogonal?
choices: the rows of $Q$ are orthogonal but any length
explanations: The rows must also have unit length.
Invertible is much weaker.
$\det Q=\pm1$ is necessary but not sufficient (e.g. a shear has $\det=1$).

questions.prompt: Every orthogonal matrix has determinant $1$.
explanations: The determinant is $\pm1$. Reflections have determinant $-1$.

questions.prompt: If $Q$ is orthogonal, then $\det Q=\pm1$.
explanations: $1=\det(Q^TQ)=(\det Q)^2$.

questions.prompt: A matrix with orthogonal (but not unit-length) columns is an orthogonal matrix.
explanations: The columns must be orthonormal. For example, $\mathrm{diag}(1,2)$ is not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: If $\det Q=1$ then $Q$ is orthogonal.
explanations: $\det=1$ is not enough: the shear $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $1$ and is not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: The product of two orthogonal matrices is orthogonal.
explanations: $(PQ)^T(PQ)=Q^TP^TPQ=Q^TQ=I$.

questions.prompt: The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is orthogonal.
explanations: $Q^{-1}=Q^T$ and $(Q^T)^TQ^T=QQ^T=I$.

questions.prompt: The sum of two orthogonal matrices is always orthogonal.
explanations: For example $I+I=2I$ is not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: Every orthogonal matrix is symmetric.
explanations: A rotation by $90^\circ$ is orthogonal but not symmetric.

questions.prompt: A permutation matrix is orthogonal.
explanations: Its columns are the standard basis vectors in some order, which are orthonormal.

questions.prompt: The identity matrix is orthogonal.
explanations: $I^TI=I$.

explanations: Orthogonal matrices do not stretch.
Length is not squared.
$\det Q$ can be $-1$, and lengths are never negative; $\|Q\mathbf x\|=\|\mathbf x\|$.

questions.prompt: Which identity proves $\|Q\mathbf x\|=\|\mathbf x\|$?
explanations: The determinant does not appear.
$(Q\mathbf x)^T=\mathbf x^TQ^T$, so the middle factor is $Q^TQ$.
The transpose of $Q\mathbf x$ is $\mathbf x^TQ^T$, not $\mathbf x^TQ$.

questions.prompt: If $Q$ is orthogonal, then $(Q\mathbf x)\cdot(Q\mathbf y)=$
explanations: Only perpendicular vectors have zero dot product.
The sign is preserved; orthogonal matrices keep dot products.
The dot product is a number, not a vector you can multiply by $Q$.

questions.prompt: Because orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and dot products, they also preserve
explanations: Entries change (rotations move vectors).
Eigenvalues change unless the matrix is special.
Angles are computed from dot products and lengths, both preserved.

explanations: Only the identity does that.
Projections shrink lengths and are not invertible.
They are invertible, so $\det\neq0$.

explanations: Projections are not invertible.
Reflections have $\det=-1$.
Shears are not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: A $2\times2$ orthogonal matrix with $\det=-1$ is
explanations: Stretches are not orthogonal.
Rotations have $\det=1$.
The identity has $\det=1$.

explanations: A reflection is not a rotation.
$-R$ times $R$ is $-R^2$.

questions.prompt: The set of vectors $\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^n$. The matrix $U=[\mathbf u_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf u_n]$ is
explanations: Nothing forces the entries off the diagonal to vanish.
Orthonormal vectors are independent, so $U$ is invertible.

explanations: That is $1$.
That is the squared length of $\mathbf x$.
That is one number, not a coordinate along $\mathbf u_i$.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an orthogonal matrix?
explanations: The columns are orthogonal but have length $5$. Divide by $5$ and it is orthogonal.
The second column has length $2$.

explanations: The columns are not perpendicular and not unit length.
The columns are not perpendicular: dot product $4\neq0$.
The columns are orthogonal but have length $\sqrt5$. It needs the factor $1/\sqrt5$.

explanations: $\sqrt{9}/3=1$, not $\sqrt3$.
Column 1 is $(1,2,2)/3$ with length $\sqrt{1+4+4}/3=1$.

explanations: That is $Q$ itself.
That is $-Q^T$, so it would give $-I$.

$Q\mathbf x=(3,4)$; $3$ is just one coordinate.

questions.prompt: $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $B^TB=$
explanations: The diagonal entries are the squared lengths $2$.
That is $I$. Column lengths are $\sqrt2$, not $1$.

questions.prompt: What scalar $c$ makes $cB$ orthogonal, where $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$?
explanations: That makes columns longer.
$(cB)^T(cB)=2c^2I$, so $c^2=\tfrac12$.

questions.prompt: For $Q=\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt2&0\\1/\sqrt2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ (3×2), $Q^TQ=$
explanations: The columns are unit vectors, so the diagonal is $1$.
$Q^TQ$ is $2\times2$ here.
That is the upper block of $QQ^T$, not $Q^TQ$.

questions.prompt: For the same $Q$ (3×2 with orthonormal columns), $QQ^T$ is
explanations: It projects onto col$(Q)$; it is nonzero.
$Q$ is $3\times2$, so $QQ^T$ is $3\times3$.
It has rank $2$, so it cannot be $I_3$.

questions.prompt: For the same $Q$ and $\mathbf b=(1,3,5)$, the projection of $\mathbf b$ onto col$(Q)$ is
explanations: $Q^T\mathbf b$ has two entries; the projection $QQ^T\mathbf b$ has three.
That is $Q^T\mathbf b$, a vector in $\mathbb R^2$.
That is $\mathbf b$ itself, which is not in col$(Q)$.

questions.prompt: If $Q$ has orthonormal columns, the least-squares solution of $Q\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is
explanations: Sizes do not match ($Q$ is $m\times n$).
$\hat{\mathbf x}$ lives in $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathbf b$ in $\mathbb R^m$.
$QQ^T$ is generally singular.

explanations: The right side must be $Q^T\mathbf b$.
That says $A\hat{\mathbf x}=\mathbf b$, which need not be solvable.
Orders swapped.

explanations: Orthogonal matrices need not be symmetric.

choices: rotate/reflect, stretch along the axes, rotate/reflect

questions.explanation: $Q$ is symmetric and orthogonal, so $Q^{-1}=Q^T=Q$, with $(1,1)$ entry $1/3$.
